strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in DiT-based SR quantization, with clear identification of three key technical challenges
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four real-world benchmarks with multiple metrics and detailed ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Technically sound methods combining Hadamard transforms, rate-distortion analysis, and dynamic programming in a principled framework
Practical value with minimal calibration requirements (32 images) and significant compression gains (5.8× size, 6.14× FLOPs at W4A4)

weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—individual components (hierarchical SVD, variance-based mixed precision, temporal scheduling) are applications of established techniques; primary novelty is domain-specific rather than methodological

Marginal and inconsistent improvements over recent baselines: on RealSR W4A6, Q-DiT4SR LPIPS (0.3386) underperforms SVDQuant (0.3371); many metrics show competitive but not consistently superior results

Critical evaluation concern: paper acknowledges that methods with 'visibly noisy reconstructions' achieve high no-reference metric scores (MANIQA), suggesting fundamental metric-quality mismatch; no user studies validate perceptual improvements

Insufficient theoretical depth: PCA analysis (Fig. 4) limited to single layer; lacks clear explanation of why block-wise rank-1 SVD preserves details; Gaussian assumptions in Eq. 13 not rigorously validated for SR domain
Overclaimed results: 'SOTA performance' claim not uniformly supported across datasets and metrics; primarily competitive rather than clearly dominant
Missing experimental analysis: no sensitivity to calibration set size, block size selection not detailed, no exploration of very aggressive quantization (W3A3), no failure case analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with three concrete challenges in DiT-based SR quantization clearly articulated
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets with multiple metrics (LPIPS, MUSIQ, MANIQA, ClipIQA, LIQE) and extensive baselines
Solid mathematical framework grounded in rate-distortion theory with good empirical motivation (PCA analysis in Fig. 4 and variance distribution analysis in Figs. 5-6)
Thorough ablation studies examining H-SVD rank budget, VaSMP cross-layer allocation, and VaTMP temporal scheduling contributions
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and comprehensive related work section
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: H-SVD combines existing global SVD with block-wise rank-1 approximation (incremental over SVDQuant); VaSMP applies standard variance-based allocation; VaTMP uses known DP-based scheduling. Contribution is primarily engineering integration rather than methodological innovation

Marginal and inconsistent improvements: Table 1 shows improvements of 1-3% over SVDQuant, with Q-DiT4SR sometimes underperforming (e.g., RealSR LPIPS 0.3386 vs SVDQuant 0.3371). Many baseline methods achieve comparable performance

Critical evaluation reliability issue: Paper acknowledges that no-reference IQA metrics (MUSIQ, MANIQA, ClipIQA, LIQE) show misalignment with perceptual quality in heavily quantized diffusion models but does not resolve this, weakening confidence in main results
Overclaimed contributions: 'Data-free' VaSMP still requires FP model statistics; 'minimal calibration' VaTMP uses 32 images; 'first PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR' is a narrow claim with limited scope
Limited generalization: Only tested on single backbone (DiT4SR); unclear if H-SVD block size search generalizes to other architectures; calibration set specific to RealSR training split

Insufficient technical justification: No ablation on rank-1 choice for SVD-L blocks; greedy discretization in VaSMP lacks optimality proof; piecewise-constant restriction in VaTMP not justified; why rank 32 for SVD-G is arbitrary
Reproducibility concerns: Code not provided at review time; some hyperparameters lack justification; would be difficult to reproduce without released code

Incomplete comparisons: No comparison with quantization-aware training approaches; comparisons with concurrent 2025 methods (PassionSR, QueST) make it unclear if improvements are genuine advances or just different design choices

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on multiple real-world SR benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250) under aggressive W4A4 quantization with impressive 5.8× size and 6.14× ops reduction

Comprehensive experimental validation with 11 baseline comparisons, thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4), and multiple analysis tools (PCA, frequency domain, variance distribution, DP scheduling heatmaps)

Well-motivated technical approach with solid theoretical grounding: H-SVD hierarchical decomposition combining global and local structures is elegant; VaSMP uses rate-distortion theory for data-free weight allocation; VaTMP employs DP for temporal activation scheduling

Practical efficiency advantage with minimal calibration requirements: VaSMP is completely calibration-free, VaTMP needs only 32 small images (128×128 crops), significantly better than methods requiring extensive calibration
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figs. 2-3, 7-9) that effectively communicate problem motivation and technical contributions
Honest discussion of evaluation limitations (Section 4.2) regarding metric reliability mismatch with perceptual quality in quantized diffusion models
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to single DiT4SR backbone with no evaluation on other DiT-based SR models (DreamClear, etc.); generalization to other architectures remains unclear

Moderate novelty composed primarily of combining existing techniques: H-SVD extends prior SVD residual quantization work; Hadamard-based activation quantization from Yang et al. 2025; variance-based allocation parallels HAWQ. Main contribution is effective combination rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient design justification: (1) Why specifically rank-1 for local blocks in H-SVD rather than other ranks? (2) Constraint in Eq. 9 uses ≲ with unclear tolerance; (3) Calibration set selection has no sensitivity analysis despite relying on statistics {v_ℓ,t}
Evaluation concerns: acknowledged metric reliability issues (MANIQA gives high scores to noisy quantized outputs); no proposed solutions; LPIPS unavailable for practical deployments
Limited quantization regime exploration: only W4A4 and W4A6 tested; no exploration of W3A3, extremely aggressive W2A2, or other configurations; unclear scaling behavior

VaTMP formulation underspecified: lacks pseudocode, complexity analysis missing, 'piecewise-constant schedule' constraint not formally defined, optimal clipping threshold A*(b) computation unclear, calibration set size sensitivity unexplored

Missing critical experiments: no evaluation on other DiT models, no actual hardware latency measurements (only FLOPs), no comparison with QAT methods or orthogonal compression approaches (pruning, distillation), no calibration overhead comparison across methods
Reproducibility issues: code URL incomplete on page 1, block size search strategy (Eq. 8) complexity unstated, implementation details of {v_ℓ,t} collection/aggregation underspecified

strengths: First systematic PTQ framework specifically designed for DiT-based Real-ISR, addressing a timely and practical gap in literature
Well-motivated hierarchical SVD combining global low-rank and local block-wise rank-1 branches, with clear theoretical grounding in rate-distortion theory for variance-aware mixed precision
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 real-world benchmarks with 6 metrics each, thorough ablation studies validating each component, and practical efficiency measurements
Strong SOTA results under both W4A6 and W4A4 settings with meaningful compression (5.8× size, 6.14× FLOPs) and verified end-to-end speedup (4.51×)
Data-free VaSMP and calibration-minimal VaTMP strategies that reduce deployment overhead compared to prior quantization methods
Honest discussion of limitations including W4A4 artifacts, speedup vs FLOPs gap, and metric reliability issues, demonstrating research integrity
Generalization studies on DreamClear architecture and calibration robustness analysis across different domains (Table 8)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components - Hadamard transforms, low-rank SVD, and rate-distortion theory for bit allocation are primarily adapted from prior work, making contributions somewhat incremental

Significant gap between theoretical FLOPs reduction (6.14×) and practical end-to-end speedup (4.51×), with H-SVD branches and nonlinear operations becoming bottlenecks that limit real-world deployment benefits
Non-trivial quality degradation under W4A4, the most aggressive and practical regime, particularly on generalization (DreamClear LIQE: 3.082→2.715), limiting applicability
Incomplete ablation studies: rank-1 for SVD-L blocks not justified; only limited exploration of block sizes; no comparison with alternative decomposition strategies
Gaussian assumption for Hadamard-transformed activations (Eq. 1) stated with unspecified assumptions; high-rate approximation (Eq. 12) questionable for 4-bit quantization
Acknowledged metric reliability issues where heavily quantized poor-quality outputs still score relatively high on no-reference IQA metrics (Section 4.2), undermining W4A4 evaluation confidence
Limited experimental scope - only ×4 upsampling tested; generalization demonstrated on single alternative architecture (DreamClear) with degradation; no QAT comparison

Implementation details under-specified: Triton kernel for SVD-L efficiency claims need more detail; native arbitrary-precision kernel unavailability limits practical benefit of sophisticated scheduling strategies

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates why existing quantization methods fail for DiT-based SR through loss of fine-grained texture details
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive benchmarks (4 real-world datasets), diverse metrics, thorough ablation studies, and practical speedup profiling
Practical efficiency gains: achieves meaningful 5.8× compression and 6.14× operation reduction at W4A4 with competitive quality on multiple settings
Minimal calibration overhead: VaSMP is calibration-free and VaTMP requires only 32 images, making the approach practical
Thoughtful presentation: generally clear writing with informative figures, particularly the frequency analysis (Fig. 2) and temporal scheduling visualization (Fig. 9)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: H-SVD combines existing global low-rank and local rank-1 SVD without principled justification for rank-1 choice; VaSMP/VaTMP are straightforward applications of rate-distortion theory and dynamic programming—mostly engineering rather than methodological innovation

Inconsistent W4A4 experimental results undermine main claims: on DrealSR, Q-DiT4SR LPIPS (0.4327) is worse than SVDQuant (0.3821); on RealSR, SVDQuant (0.3268) outperforms Q-DiT4SR (0.3665)—claimed SOTA performance does not hold consistently

Acknowledged metric reliability issues directly contradict evaluation rigor: paper notes some methods with 'visibly noisy reconstructions' score high on MANIQA; suspicious W4A6 improvements over FP (e.g., Table 7: 62.94 vs 57.77) suggest metrics fail to reflect true quality

Significant reproducibility gaps: block size search procedure not detailed, clipping threshold computation (Eq. 19) method missing, DP formulation for VaTMP sparse, calibration sensitivity on 32-image sets unexplored, code unavailable at review

Questionable mathematical assumptions: Gaussian assumption for Hadamard-transformed activations (Eq. 1) not rigorously validated empirically; rate-distortion derivation (Eq. 12-13) validity under aggressive W4A4 quantization unestablished

H-SVD design lacks principled justification: Figure 4 (PCA analysis) does not justify rank-1 blocks over rank-2/3; block size selection via loose inequality (Eq. 9) admits multiple valid configurations with no principled selection criterion

Practical speedup gap undermines utility: theoretical 6.14× vs measured 4.51× speedup; acknowledged lack of native W3A3/W5A5 kernel support means speedup numbers may not reflect real deployment; memory overhead (3974.64 MiB) exceeds SVDQuant (3722.83 MiB) for comparable speedup
Limited architectural generalization: only two DiT models tested (DiT4SR + brief DreamClear evaluation); W4A4 generalization on DreamClear shows concerning LPIPS degradation (0.3752 vs 0.3249 FP)

Acknowledged artifact limitations without solutions (Sec. 4.6): acknowledges failures on thin/repetitive/high-contrast textures under W4A4 but proposes no mitigation; Table 9 shows only modest improvements (Edge MAE 0.2235 vs baseline 0.2757)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of three key challenges (detail preservation, inter-layer sensitivity, temporal dynamics) in DiT-based SR quantization
Solid theoretical grounding in rate-distortion theory for VaSMP and principled DP formulation for VaTMP, though with some unvalidated assumptions
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 real-world datasets with diverse metrics, thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4), and practical runtime analysis
Strong empirical results consistently outperforming diverse baselines (SVDQuant, QuaRot, Q-DiT, PassionSR) under W4A6 and W4A4 settings with minimal visual degradation
Practical efficiency with minimal calibration overhead: VaSMP requires zero calibration data, VaTMP needs only 32 LR images
Honest discussion of limitations including metric-quality mismatch, W4A4 artifacts, and practical speedup gap; includes artifact analysis rather than hiding degradation
Generalization test on DreamClear and calibration robustness analysis (Table 8) demonstrating some transferability
Clear problem motivation supported by insightful analysis (PCA analysis in Fig. 4, variance distribution in Fig. 5)
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty: Hadamard transforms and SVD-based decomposition are directly adapted from recent work; novelty lies primarily in combination for specific domain rather than conceptual innovation

Theoretical gaps in core components: high-rate approximation validity at 4-bit precision unexamined, Gaussian assumption stated but not empirically validated, greedy discretization has no optimality guarantees
H-SVD hyperparameter exploration insufficient: only tested with rank-32 SVD-G and rank-8 SVD-L; matched parameter budget constraint (Eq. 9) lacks theoretical justification

Evaluation methodology concerns: authors acknowledge that quantized models with visibly noisy outputs score well on no-reference metrics (MANIQA), undermining confidence in quantitative results; visual comparisons cherry-picked; W4A6 improvements over FP unexplained
Significant practical speedup gap: theoretical 6.14× ops reduction achieves only 4.51× end-to-end speedup with no proposed solutions; nonlinear operations become bottleneck
Limited scope and generalization: main results on DiT4SR only with DreamClear showing weaker W4A4 results; only ×4 upscaling tested; scalability to different model sizes unclear

Incomplete practical details: active set A determination mechanism unclear, VaTMP DP computational cost unquantified, block size search complexity not analyzed, sensitivity to calibration set size not studied

Activation quantization relies on unvalidated Gaussian assumption without empirical verification on actual DiT models; optimal clipping threshold computation (Eq. 19) assumes normality without checking
Claims 'data-free' VaSMP misleadingly—requires FP model weight statistics which implicitly encode dataset information
Missing runtime comparisons with baseline methods on same hardware; only theoretical ops reduction provided, making it difficult to assess practical advantages over SVDQuant (4.8× vs 4.5× speedup)
